While treatable with prompt intravenous anticonvulsants, antibiotics or antimalarials, and supportive care, delay can lead to brain damage or death. Please rush the child to the nearest health centre or hospital right now for proper diagnosis and injection-based treatment if indicated.

An elderly man came to our local hospital. This man said he has a severe headache, his neck is stiff, and he has rashes suddenly appearing on his body. He came to ask what could be causing it and what kind of treatment can be given to him.
We asked the man whether the headache started suddenly or if it came gradually. The man said it started suddenly at night and has become very severe now. We also asked him if he can look at light properly, and he said no, because light affects his head and makes the headache worse.

This presentation—severe sudden headache, neck stiffness, light sensitivity, and an itchy widespread rash—is highly suggestive of acute bacterial meningitis, most likely meningococcal meningitis with meningococcemia, which is an infectious emergency.  
The patient needs an immediate lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid analysis (cell count, Gram stain, culture), plus blood cultures and a full blood count; if available, a rapid meningococcal antigen test can speed diagnosis.  
While awaiting results, start empiric intravenous antibiotics without delay—ceftriaxone is preferred if accessible, otherwise use benzylpenicillin plus chloramphenicol per local protocols for suspected bacterial meningitis.  
Supportive care is essential: give analgesia, maintain hydration, and monitor closely.  
Isolate the patient, and if meningococcal disease is confirmed, close contacts should receive chemoprophylaxis (e.g., ciprofloxacin) as per your local public health guidelines.

model_answer: This pattern of coughing fits ending with a desperate struggle to breathe strongly suggests pertussis (whooping cough), a highly contagious bacterial infection of the airways. The intense coughing paroxysms are caused by *Bordetella pertussis*, which produces thick mucus and inflammation, leaving the child gasping for air with a characteristic “whoop” or post-tussive breathlessness and often vomiting. In our community setting, incomplete or waning vaccination coverage makes pertussis a common cause of such abrupt, severe spells. You should bring the child to the hospital immediately for assessment, a nasopharyngeal swab, and early antibiotics like erythromycin to reduce severity and transmission. We will also provide supportive care, including gentle airway suctioning and monitoring for complications like pneumonia or apnea.
